fields.title: Tropa: The Product Is Better, But They Don't Switch
fields.summary: Thirty salons in the pilot, only eight are active users. The team suggests adding features. Decide what to do.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do during this month before the launch decision?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for Tropa.
fields.brief/company: Tropa is a fictional online booking service for barbershops and salons with 2–6 stylists.
fields.brief/context: Three months ago, you onboarded 30 salons into a pilot. Eight use it actively. The team proposes adding a loyalty program and client reminders—features the closest competitor lacks. You have one month before the full launch decision.
fields.brief/objective: Understand why they aren't switching and decide what to do before launch.
fields.brief/constraints: Two developers, a designer, and you. No researcher—you'll have to talk to users yourself.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you will do during this month and justify your choice.
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Switching depends on four forces at once, and adding features only strengthens one of them. As long as the basic task is cheaper in the old way, and the fear of failure isn't resolved, objective superiority won't move anyone. Look at how the task is solved now and what the user stands to lose if the new tool fails—that is usually your work for the coming month.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
30 salons onboarded, 8 use it regularly (more than half of appointments are booked through the product).

Breakdown by size: out of 8 active, seven are salons with 4–6 stylists. Out of 22 inactive, nineteen have 2–3 stylists.

Breakdown by onboarding date: the first ten salons onboarded with a personal visit from the founder; 5 of them are active. The next twenty onboarded self-serve using instructions; 3 are active.

The product tracks the event 'appointment created', but lacks the event 'appointment created manually by admin instead of client': they are indistinguishable.

Average stylist workload between active and inactive salons differs by 2%.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
You visited four inactive salons.

Appointments are kept in a paper notebook at the front desk. Clients message via Instagram Direct or call; the admin writes it down in the notebook.

When asked what's wrong with the notebook, all four replied that it suits them completely.

One admin said: 'When a stylist got sick, I called everyone off the notebook in two minutes. In the app, I don't know what will happen.'

In all four salons, the app was installed and logged into—during the first week.

In two salons, a printed flyer with a QR code 'Book online' given at onboarding was lying on the counter. In neither salon was it in a visible spot.
fields.evidenceCards/2/title: What They Say vs. What They Do
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Survey across all 30 salons, 19 responded.

'Do you like the product?'—84% positive answers.
'Do you plan to keep using it?'—79% yes.

Yet only eight out of thirty actually use it.

In conversations, owners cite reasons for delaying: 'haven't gotten around to it', 'need to get the admin to figure it out', 'it's peak season, no time right now'.

One owner stated directly: 'If booking breaks on Saturday, I lose a day's revenue. The notebook doesn't break.'

No one explained what happens to the notebook during transition: it's not in the instructions.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The admin works shifts, often being one of the stylists.

Rescheduling an appointment: client messages via Direct → admin checks notebook → replies → writes it down. Takes one minute.

In the product, rescheduling takes 4 steps and requires the client to exist in the system. If the client booked by phone, they must be created manually.

Payment—in cash or by transfer to the stylist. The product doesn't know this and shows the visit as unpaid.

Salons with 4–6 stylists have a dedicated admin; salons with 2–3 stylists have no dedicated admin—whoever is free takes the booking.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Analyze forces of switch and ease anxiety
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Find out what job the notebook was hired for and address retaining forces: show what happens during outages, allow parallel usage, make rescheduling no slower than one minute in the notebook.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Conversations about the last specific rescheduled appointment give an accurate picture: in the notebook it takes a minute, in the product—four steps and creating a client manually. The pull of the new tool doesn't matter while the core action cost is higher.
Rescheduling is reduced to two steps, and phone bookings are allowed without client data—four days of dev work.
A 'what to do if internet goes down' section is added to instructions, and salons are allowed to keep the paper notebook in parallel for the first month. This removes the spoken fear of losing Saturday revenue.
Within a month, nine of the 22 inactive salons start using the app, six of which have 2–3 stylists.
The loyalty program is postponed: not a single salon asked for it.
Trade-off: you did nothing the team suggested, and the month looked like polishing minor details.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The competitor lacks this. Build a loyalty program and automated client reminders—this will increase product appeal.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Both features launch in a month. Out of eight active salons, three enable loyalty and six enable reminders; active users love it.
Not a single salon out of the 22 inactive ones starts using the app: rescheduling is still more costly than in the notebook, and fear of failure remains.
At full launch, the same pattern repeats: salons onboard eagerly, few actually use it.
During post-mortem, someone notes that no salon ever asked for loyalty—the idea came from comparing features with a competitor.
Trade-off: you increased the pull for those who had already switched, leaving untouched what was holding back the rest.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: People say 'we need to get the admin to figure it out'. Conduct training sessions across all 22 salons.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Training takes three weeks: one hour per salon plus commute.
There is an effect, but small: four salons start using it, all with 4–6 stylists and a dedicated admin.
In salons with 2–3 stylists, there is no one to train: whoever is free handles bookings, and next week someone else is at the desk.
Rescheduling still takes four steps, so even trained staff return to the notebook on busy days.
Trade-off: you mistook a difference in task cost for a lack of knowledge, spending a month on the most labor-intensive approach.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Calculate model and optimize for impact
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Estimate which lever yields more: conversion to onboarded, share of active users, or appointments per salon—and focus on the most sensitive one.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The calculation takes an hour and yields the right answer: active user share is the most sensitive multiplier; onboarding new salons is useless while only a quarter switch.
This shuts down the team's proposal to launch to a wide base and sets the right priority.
However, the model doesn't answer why they aren't switching. The month ends with clear priorities but no actionable plan.
Trade-off: you got the right goal without getting closer to the root cause.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Customer described via demographics rather than tasks and struggles
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Gathered facts aren't synthesized, leaving blind spots hidden
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Behavior is explained by persona rather than situation
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Failed to uncover current solution and why it persists
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: End-to-end journey ignored: steps outside the product remain unseen
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Looking for causes in front-stage UI when they stem from back-stage operations
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: Guessing hypotheses endlessly instead of decomposing metrics and segmenting
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: Analyzing aggregate metrics without cohorts while user mix shifts
fields.rubric/remediation/8/gap: Effect size wasn't estimated before starting work
